title: Going beyond RAG: Extended Mind Transformers - Phoebe Klett

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The primary object is the Transformer architecture itself—an attention edit enabling internal retrieval—and its intrinsic behavior including causal citations and hallucination reduction, rather than an external retrieval system or serving infrastructure.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The primary object is the Transformer architecture itself—an attention edit enabling internal retrieval—and its intrinsic behavior including causal citations and hallucination reduction, rather than an external retrieval system or serving infrastructure.

summary: Extended Mind Transformers (EMT) address limitations of both long-context and RAG approaches. Long context requires expensive fine-tuning and can confuse models with irrelevant information; RAG makes relevance choices once upfront using coarse representations disjoint from how the model reasons. EMT instead exploits the Transformer's existing key/value retrieval mechanism: memory tokens are passed through the model to save key-value representations per decoder layer, then during generation each query token retrieves memory tokens via cosine similarity and attends to them. This is a simple attention edit; the hard part is position assignment. Prior work needed fine-tuning due to absolute position embeddings, but modern relative embeddings—RoPE (Llama) and ALiBi (Mosaic MPT)—enable EMT without fine-tuning. Evaluations use a new open-sourced counterfactual retrieval benchmark (2k–16k token contexts) controlling for memorized facts by replacing correct answers with plausible wrong ones. EMT models, not fine-tuned, stay competitive with fine-tuned long-context models through 16k and outperform GPT-4 when seeded with RAG context. Fine-tuning on long contexts degrades attention quality on shorter inputs. EMT enables granular causal citations: you can identify exactly which memory tokens were retrieved and attended to for a generated token. It also reduces hallucinations via an active-learning-inspired mechanism: detect token uncertainty (e.g., entropy) and regenerate with more retrieved memory tokens. Key implementation parameters include stride length (smaller stride yields higher-quality representations but more computation) and top K (the number of memory key-value pairs each query token retrieves, which should scale with memory length). Two regularization techniques improve quality: similarity masking discards retrieved tokens below a cosine similarity threshold (e.g., 0.25), and unknown-token elimination removes poorly represented tokens that spuriously match queries—especially important for RoPE models on messy data like Wikipedia benchmarks. Models and code are open-sourced on Hugging Face and GitHub; memories can be passed as input tokens at model instantiation and dynamically changed afterward, requiring only proper config setup.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Intro and problem framing
sections.summary: Phoebe introduces herself and the talk agenda. Long context and RAG solve loading application-specific information differently with different downsides: long context is expensive to fine-tune and can confuse the model; RAG makes relevance choices once upfront with coarse representations disjoint from model reasoning. Distinguishing memory from inference query enables granular citations and active retrieval.

sections.title: Extended Mind attention method
sections.summary: EMT is a simple attention edit: pass memory tokens through the model saving per-layer key-value pairs, then let each query token retrieve memory tokens via cosine similarity and attend to them. Position assignment is the hard part; prior work needed fine-tuning due to absolute embeddings, but RoPE (Llama) and ALiBi (Mosaic MPT) enable EMT without fine-tuning.

sections.title: Evaluations and counterfactual benchmark
sections.summary: A new open-source counterfactual retrieval benchmark uses 2k–16k token contexts and replaces correct answers with plausible wrong ones to control for memorized facts. EMT (not fine-tuned) stays competitive with fine-tuned long-context models through 16k, and outperforms GPT-4 when seeded with RAG context. Fine-tuning on long contexts degrades attention on shorter inputs.

sections.title: Citations
sections.summary: Unlike RAG's post-hoc rationalization citations, EMT can identify exactly which memory tokens were retrieved and attended to for each generated token, providing causal citations. Example with Alexander Grothendieck query shows retrieved tokens including '1971'.

sections.title: Reducing hallucinations via uncertainty
sections.summary: Token-level entropy (or Bayesian fine-tuning uncertainty) can detect uncertain generation steps; when detected, regenerate using more memory tokens. Example shows default retrieval giving wrong answer (1993) but increased retrieval on uncertainty giving correct (1971).

sections.title: Implementation parameters
sections.summary: Stride length controls how much context each memory token sees when generating representations: smaller stride yields higher-quality representations but more computation. Top K is the most important parameter—the number of memory key-value pairs each query token retrieves and attends to—dynamically set based on memory length. Two regularization techniques improve quality: similarity masking discards retrieved tokens below a cosine similarity threshold (e.g., 0.25), and unknown-token elimination removes poorly represented tokens that spuriously match queries, especially important for RoPE models on messy data like Wikipedia benchmarks.

sections.title: Conclusion and resources
sections.summary: Models are available on Hugging Face with code and dataset on GitHub. Using EMT is straightforward: pass memories as input tokens at model instantiation (dynamically changeable afterward) and configure the model config properly. Phoebe concludes that EMT achieves impressive retrieval performance, enables causal citations and active-learning-inspired hallucination reduction, requires no fine-tuning, and is easy to deploy with open-source models and code.
